case_study_insert.main_stem: Portwyn Container Services (PCS) is a public limited company in the port handling and shipping sector, employing a workforce of 190 at the Port of Dunmere. Founded in 1996, the company is led by chief executive Devika Menon and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership, handling import and export containers for international shipping lines. PCS plans to invest $1,250,000 in two ship-to-shore gantry cranes and a six-acre yard expansion, financed by a $750,000 share issue and a $500,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $480,000 a year, a variable cost of $18.50 a unit and a selling price of $26.50, and produces 95,000 units a year (each unit being one container lifted). PCS faces rising crane operator fatigue, with near-miss safety incidents reaching 7 last quarter.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Safety Report — Q3 2026: The terminal lifted 24,800 containers last quarter with a crane defect rate of 2.3%, down from 3.6% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 41 to 26 per month. Average gate-to-gate turnaround time is 3.1 hours. A survey of 280 shipping line clients found that 67% would commit to longer contracts if dwell time fell below 48 hours, and 61% rated yard automation as their top priority. Fatigue monitoring shows 18 of 190 staff regularly work over 60 hours a week. Off-the-job crane simulator courses cost $1,100 per operator.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Portwyn Container Services for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.0%, increasing borrowing costs for variable-rate debt. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $13.10 to $13.91 per hour from April 2027, raising terminal labour costs. (3) Steel and container-handling equipment costs have risen 14.8% year-on-year, while import volumes through the Port of Dunmere grew 3.4% and congestion surcharges fell 5.5%.

questions.question_text: PCS plans to finance its $1,250,000 crane and yard expansion partly with a $750,000 share issue. Explain two advantages for PCS of using a share issue to fund the expansion instead of the $500,000 bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue brings in $750,000 of finance that never has to be repaid and carries no mandatory interest, which is ideal while PCS already pays interest payable of $70,000–$84,000 a year and has just taken on a $500,000 bank loan. Unlike a loan, share proceeds strengthen the equity base that supports the two new $1,250,000 gantry cranes, improving solvency and giving lenders confidence, and leaving PCS headroom to borrow again if a third crane or further yard automation becomes attractive.

Point 2: Selling new shares spreads ownership rather than concentrating risk with Devika Menon and existing shareholders, and public investors in a public limited company are usually comfortable funding infrastructure that earns returns over a long horizon. Crucially, a share issue avoids fixed repayment pressure during the years the cranes are being commissioned, when lift volumes and the 2.3% defect rate are still stabilising — the exact period when a $500,000 loan with interest already stretching to $84,000 could bite. No collateral is pledged against the yard, and the democratic board can present the issue as a growth story tied to the 67% of clients willing to sign longer contracts if dwell time improves.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to PCS's financing, expansion and crane commissioning.

questions.question_text: PCS is promoting its expanded handling capacity and faster gate-to-gate turnaround to international shipping lines. Consider sponsoring a major ports industry conference, a series of trade-press adverts in shipping publications, or hosting open-house tours of the new yard for 280 client contacts. Which should PCS choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Ports industry conference sponsorship: Sponsoring a major ports conference puts PCS in front of hundreds of shipping executives at once and confers prestige beside national competitors. It would publicise the $1,250,000 crane investment and the 3.1-hour turnaround quickly. However, headline sponsorship is expensive for a 190-employee terminal already carrying a $750,000 share issue and $500,000 bank loan, much of the audience is suppliers or rivals rather than buyers, and the message is one-directional with no guarantee of contract signatures.

Trade-press advertising: Regular adverts in shipping publications reach procurement decision-makers across the industry, reinforce the 67% dwell-time promise and 61% automation research, and are cheaper and more repeatable than a one-off conference. The drawback is low interaction: readers may not respond, and abstract claims about faster turnaround are less convincing than seeing the cranes operate.

Open-house tours of the new yard: Hosting the 280 surveyed shipping line clients lets them see the two gantry cranes, watch 3.1-hour turnaround in reality, meet fatigue-safe shift managers and discuss longer contracts directly — precisely addressing the 67% who said they would commit if dwell time fell below 48 hours. Tours are highly persuasive but time-consuming, reach limited numbers per day, and repeated events could disrupt 24-hour terminal operations.

Recommendation: PCS should choose open-house tours of the new yard, supported by targeted trade-press advertising. Live demonstration is the most powerful proof for sceptical shipping lines and converts directly on the 48-hour dwell-time promise where PCS has a genuine edge. Conference sponsorship is rejected as high-cost, low-target awareness; trade press alone is rejected as too passive to close contracts, though it should run alongside tours to sustain visibility between events.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of promotional options with minimal application to PCS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of at least two options in the context of PCS with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of PCS with a well-justified recommendation explaining why conference sponsorship and trade press alone are rejected.

questions.question_text: PCS faces rising crane operator fatigue, with near-miss safety incidents reaching 7 last quarter and 18 of 190 staff working over 60 hours a week. Explain two benefits for PCS of introducing job rotation between crane operators and yard staff.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Job rotation widens each operator's skill set between crane cabins, yard planning and gate administration, breaking the physical and mental monotony that drives fatigue on long shifts. Rotating staff across roles means no one stares at spreader loads for twelve hours straight, directly attacking the fatigue flagged by monitoring — 18 staff regularly working over 60 hours — and reducing the chance of the next near-miss beyond the 7 recorded last quarter.

Point 2: Rotation creates a flexible, multi-skilled crew able to cover absences and peak sailings without mandatory overtime, lowering the overtime burden that is already exhausting staff and lifting labour costs. It also strengthens team working under PCS's democratic leadership, gives staff new variety that supports motivation and retention across the 190 employees, and improves continuity when the two new gantry cranes enter service, so lift quality stays high while training on the new machines is absorbed across the whole shift team rather than concentrated on a few tired operators.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to PCS's fatigue, safety incidents and crane commissioning.

questions.question_text: PCS must cut crane operator fatigue and eliminate near-miss safety incidents. Consider introducing team working with quality circles for crane and yard crews, or a bonus scheme paying crews for every verified zero near-miss week. Which should PCS choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Team working with quality circles: Quality circles would bring crane operators, yard planners and supervisors together weekly to identify fatigue risks — shift patterns, cabin ergonomics, spreader signals — and propose solutions democratically. This fits PCS's democratic leadership under Devika Menon, empowers the 190 staff who actually run the cranes, and builds lasting safety habits rather than short-term compliance. Limitations: meetings take paid time out of already stretched shifts, quieter staff may not speak up, and benefits arrive gradually rather than stopping the next near-miss tomorrow.

Zero near-miss bonus scheme: A team bonus for each verified zero near-miss week is simple, immediately motivating and directly targets the 7 incidents recorded last quarter. Bonuses are highly visible and focus behaviour on safe lifting. However, cash bonuses alone can encourage under-reporting of incidents to keep payments flowing, do nothing about root causes such as fatigue from 60-hour weeks, and set an expensive precedent if every crew expects payment for ordinary safe work.

Decision: PCS should choose team working with quality circles, with a modest recognition element layered on top. It attacks the root causes of fatigue and near-misses, suits democratic leadership, involves the 18 over-worked staff in fixing their own shift design, and builds a durable safety culture as the new cranes arrive. A pure bonus scheme is rejected as the main tool because it risks silencing incident reporting and leaves exhausting 60-hour weeks untouched — the very conditions causing the 7 near-misses. Bonuses can remain a small supplement once reporting culture is trusted.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two options with limited application to PCS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both options in the context of PCS.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options in the context of PCS with a well-justified decision covering motivation, reporting culture and fatigue root causes.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how PCS's management can use its cost, break-even and lift data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $480,000 ÷ ($26.50 − $18.50) = $480,000 ÷ $8.00 = 60,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 60,000 units a year.
Formula: Margin of safety = Actual output − Break-even output. Substitution: 95,000 − 60,000 = 35,000 units. Answer: margin of safety is 35,000 units a year.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways PCS's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. With break-even at 60,000 lifts and output at 95,000 containers, PCS has a 35,000-unit margin of safety, so managers can judge how much lift volume could fall before the $1,250,000 expansion stops covering its costs — essential reassurance before committing to more cranes.
2. Contribution per unit of $8.00 lets managers model congestion-surcharge and dwell-time pricing for the 67% of clients willing to sign longer contracts, testing whether a $2 surcharge still covers the $480,000 fixed costs and $500,000 bank loan service.
3. Knowing contribution and break-even helps PCS stress-test the 14.8% rise in steel equipment costs, since pricier crane maintenance feeds the variable cost of $18.50 and squeezes the $8.00 surplus, warning managers to renegotiate shipping-line tariffs early.
4. Managers can benchmark unit cost — fixed cost per unit of $480,000 ÷ 95,000 = $5.05 plus the $18.50 variable cost, giving $23.55 a unit — to spot yard inefficiency, target the 2.3% crane defect rate, and decide whether automation investment pays back.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 60,000 units | (ii) Margin of safety = 35,000 units | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety cushion for the expansion; surcharge modelling against the $480,000 fixed costs; stress-testing the 14.8% steel cost rise; and unit-cost benchmarking at $23.55 with defect-rate reduction.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate PCS's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has PCS's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 38.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 43.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 10.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 12.0%
ROCE 2024 = 16.0%
ROCE 2025 = 17.5%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit = $5,600,000 revenue − $3,472,000 cost of sales = $2,128,000, giving $2,128,000 ÷ $5,600,000 = 38.0%; 2025 = ($6,300,000 − $3,591,000) = $2,709,000 ÷ $6,300,000 = 43.0%. After operating expenses: 2024 $560,000 ÷ $5,600,000 = 10.0%; 2025 $756,000 ÷ $6,300,000 = 12.0%. Capital efficiency: 2024 $560,000 ÷ $3,500,000 = 16.0%; 2025 $756,000 ÷ $4,320,000 = 17.5%.

Evaluation: Performance has improved on every measure. The trading margin widened from 38.0% to 43.0%, reflecting better yard automation and lower dwell-time costs, and the operating margin rose from 10.0% to 12.0% despite interest payable increasing from $70,000 to $84,000 as the $500,000 bank loan was drawn. Capital efficiency also improved from 16.0% to 17.5% even though capital employed rose by $820,000 to $4,320,000 — evidence that the yard and crane investment is already earning above its funding cost. However, cost of sales grew to $3,591,000 and the 14.8% steel price rise threatens future crane maintenance bills, while relying on longer client contracts makes PCS vulnerable if shipping volumes soften after the 3.4% import growth.

Conclusion: PCS's financial performance has improved. Trading margins strengthened from 38.0% to 43.0%, operating returns from 10.0% to 12.0% and capital efficiency from 16.0% to 17.5%, on revenue growth of $700,000. The trend is positive but fuelled by cost control and contract discipline; PCS should keep dwell time under 48 hours, hedge steel maintenance costs and avoid further debt-funded capacity until the cranes are fully commissioned.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, capital employed and interest movements and a justified conclusion on whether PCS has improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for PCS of automating yard operations with the two ship-to-shore gantry cranes.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Automation addresses the 61% of surveyed clients who rate yard automation their top priority and directly targets the 67% who would commit to longer contracts if dwell time falls below 48 hours. Faster, computer-sequenced crane cycles cut the 2.3% crane defect rate further, reduce damage claims behind the falling monthly complaints (41 to 26), and allow PCS to lift more containers with the same 190 staff — a powerful answer to labour-cost pressure from the 6.2% minimum-wage rise and to fatigue risks flagged by monitoring.

Disadvantage: The $1,250,000 automation investment raises capital employed sharply, and the two cranes will take months to commission, during which throughput may dip and disrupt the 3.1-hour turnaround that winning contracts depend on. Automation also demands new operator skills — hence the $1,100 simulator courses — and any software fault could idle both cranes at once, multiplying late lifts far beyond the 7 near-miss incidents, while staff resistance to automation could deepen tension in a democratic culture unless communication is handled carefully.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to PCS's safety, contracts and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.0%, the 6.2% increase in the minimum wage to $13.91 and the 14.8% rise in steel and equipment costs will affect PCS. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.0%): A 0.5% rise on PCS's $500,000 bank loan adds about $2,500 a year to financing costs, slightly steepening the increase in interest payable from $70,000 to $84,000 recorded in 2025. Higher rates also raise the cost of future terminal borrowing and could cool trade credit. The direct impact is small in cash terms, and PCS can fix the rate or restructure at renewal, so this is the least dangerous of the three changes.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $13.91 from April 2027): With 190 employees concentrated in crane, gate and yard roles, a 6.2% rise compounds the existing fatigue and overtime pressure. The insert gives the new floor at $13.91 per hour, up $0.81 from $13.10, so every employee paid at the minimum gains about $0.81 an hour and the terminal wage bill rises broadly across the workforce. The hours worked are not stated in the insert, so the exact annual addition cannot be quantified precisely, but it will be a recurring cost larger than the interest hit — partly recoverable through longer-contract tariffs and productivity gains from the new cranes, and valuable for morale under democratic leadership.

Steel and equipment cost inflation (14.8%): The two gantry cranes and yard automation are built from steel and imported handling equipment. A 14.8% rise on the $1,250,000 expansion would add up to roughly $185,000 to capital cost or force a cheaper specification, and the same inflation inflates ongoing crane and trailer maintenance, feeding straight into the $18.50 variable cost and the 2.3% defect-driven rework bill. It also coincides with falling congestion surcharges of 5.5%, squeezing contract pricing headroom.

Conclusion: The 14.8% rise in steel and equipment costs will have the greatest impact. It lands on the single largest commitment PCS is making — the $1,250,000 expansion itself — plus every future maintenance cycle, so it threatens both the balance sheet and the $8.00 contribution per lift. The wage increase is material but absorbable through tariffs and automation productivity, and the interest-rate rise is minor and fixable. PCS should lock in equipment prices, accelerate commissioning and renegotiate surcharge terms before April 2027.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to PCS.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on PCS's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of PCS with a well-justified judgement that steel and equipment inflation has the greatest impact.
